extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners and patent practitioners (agents/attorneys)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for identifying whether a patent claim recites an 'abstract idea' under the Alice/Mayo framework (Step 2A Prong One/Two) and how to classify claim limitations into enumerated groupings. Used by examiners when performing Section 101 eligibility analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Approach to identifying abstract ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners should determine whether a claim recites an abstract idea by (1) identifying the specific limitation(s) in the claim under examination that the examiner believes recites an abstract idea, and (2) determining whether the identified limitation(s) fall within at least one of the groupings of abstract ideas listed above.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an identified limitation falls within at least one grouping, conclude the claim recites an abstract idea in Step 2A Prong One and proceed to Step 2A Prong Two to determine whether additional elements integrate the abstract idea into a practical application (see MPEP § 2106.04(d)). If the limitations do not fall within any grouping, find the claim does not recite an abstract idea and the analysis concludes (Pathway B), except in rare circumstances (see MPEP § 2106.04(a)(3)). The groupings are not mutually exclusive; examiners should identify at least one grouping, and preferably all groupings applicable, if claim limitations fall within multiple groupings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enumerated abstract idea groupings
rubrics_metrics.description: The enumerated groupings of abstract ideas are: (1) Mathematical concepts – mathematical relationships, mathematical formulas or equations, mathematical calculations; (2) Certain methods of organizing human activity – fundamental economic principles or practices; commercial or legal interactions; managing personal behavior or relationships; and (3) Mental processes – concepts performed in the human mind (including an observation, evaluation, judgment, opinion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These groupings distill relevant case law to shift examiners from relying on individual judicial cases to applying the body of precedent across technologies and claim types. See MPEP § 2106.04(a)(2) for further discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical concepts (grouping)
rubrics_metrics.description: The mathematical concepts grouping is defined as mathematical relationships, mathematical formulas or equations, and mathematical calculations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether the claim recites a mathematical concept or merely limitations that are based on or involve a mathematical concept. A claim does not recite a mathematical concept if it is only based on or involves the concept (e.g., a particular configuration or application may avoid being an abstract idea). A mathematical concept need not be expressed in mathematical symbols; words operating on data can serve the same purpose. See cited cases (Gottschalk v. Benson; Parker v. Flook; Diamond v. Diehr; Bilski v. Kappos) and Fed. Cir. precedents (SAP America v. InvestPic; Digitech; Bancorp).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical relationships
rubrics_metrics.description: A mathematical relationship is a relationship between variables or numbers; it may be expressed in words or using mathematical symbols (e.g., pressure p = F/A).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of mathematical relationships recited in a claim include: (i) a relationship between reaction rate and temperature (Arrhenius equation); (ii) conversion between binary coded decimal and pure binary; (iii) mathematical relationship between directional radio activity and antenna conductor arrangement; (iv) organizing/manipulating information through mathematical correlations (Digitech).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical formulas or equations
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim that recites a numerical formula or equation, or a textual replacement for a formula (e.g., 'determining a ratio of A to B' or 'calculating the force by multiplying mass by acceleration'), will be considered as falling within the 'mathematical concepts' grouping.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include: formulas describing electromagnetic standing wave phenomena; the Arrhenius equation; a formula for computing an alarm limit (Flook); and a mathematical formula for hedging (Bilski). Textual descriptions that effectively define a formula should be treated as equations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical calculations
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim that recites a mathematical calculation — a mathematical operation or an act of calculating using mathematical methods to determine a variable or number — will be considered within the 'mathematical concepts' grouping when given its broadest reasonable interpretation in light of the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No particular word is required to indicate a calculation; terms like 'determining' or 'performing' may encompass mathematical calculations. Examples include: performing a resampled statistical analysis to generate a distribution; calculating an alarm limit value (Flook); using a formula to convert geospatial coordinates; managing an insurance policy via calculations (Bancorp); algorithms for visit optimization (In re Maucorps); calculating differences between local and average data values (In re Abele).

rubrics_metrics.name: Certain methods of organizing human activity (grouping)
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'methods of organizing human activity' grouping describes concepts relating to: fundamental economic principles or practices (including hedging, insurance, mitigating risk); commercial or legal interactions (including contracts, legal obligations, advertising, marketing, sales activities, business relations); and managing personal behavior or relationships or interactions between people (including social activities, teaching, following rules or instructions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The qualifier 'certain' limits this grouping: not all methods of organizing human activity are abstract ideas (e.g., a defined set of steps for combining particular ingredients to create a drug formulation is not such a method). This grouping should not be expanded beyond the enumerated sub-groupings except in rare circumstances (see MPEP § 2106.04(a)(3)). The number of people involved is not dispositive; activity involving a person and a computer may fall within this grouping. See Alice, Bilski, and related cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fundamental economic practices or principles (sub-group)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fundamental economic practices or principles encompass concepts relating to the economy and commerce, including hedging, insurance, and mitigating risk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The term 'fundamental' does not necessarily mean 'old' or 'well-known'—new methods (e.g., price optimization) may still be fundamental. Examples/cases identifying such practices include: hedging (Bilski), intermediated settlement (Alice), managing stable value protected life insurance policy (Bancorp), offer-based price optimization (OIP Techs.), and others (see list i–vii).

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial or legal interactions (sub-group)
rubrics_metrics.description: Commercial or legal interactions include agreements in the form of contracts, legal obligations, advertising, marketing or sales activities or behaviors, and business relations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An example is a transaction performance guaranty (buySAFE v. Google), where the claimed agreement was treated as a contractual relationship falling within this subgroup.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples of claims that do not recite abstract ideas (non-limiting)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some claims are not directed to an abstract idea because they do not recite an abstract idea, even if at some level they are based on or involve an abstract idea; such claims are eligible at Step 2A Prong One (Pathway B).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Non-limiting hypothetical examples given: (i) a printer comprising a belt, roller, printhead and ink cartridge; (ii) a washing machine with tub, drive motor, controller, housing; (iii) an earring with a glucose sensor and memory; (iv) a method for sequencing BRCA1 gene sequences; (v) a method for loading BIOS into a local computer system from remote memory; (vi) a method of rearranging GUI icons based on amount of use using processor-tracked memory allocation; (vii) a method of training a neural network with staged training sets. The guidance emphasizes that a claim must 'recite' (set forth or describe) an abstract idea in Prong One before moving to Prong Two.
